newsitem.title: CHINA: China fibre makers hit by prices, competition.
newsitem.headline: China fibre makers hit by prices, competition.

text.p: Surging prices for raw materials and falling prices for finished goods have squeezed China's textile fibre makers, pushing some into the red, and there is no recovery in sight this year, analysts said on Wednesday.

The latest victim of the squeeze was Shanghai Lianhua Fibre Co, which announced a net loss of 6.404 million yuan ($770,000) for first-half 1996 on Wednesday last year's net profit of 20.019 million yuan.
Yizheng Chemical Fibre, another major producer of polyester, announced a 74.2 percent drop in net profit to 212 million yuan on Monday.
"This is not a good year for China's textile fibre industry," said an analyst at one Chinese brokerage.

"The prices of raw materials have gone up and those of finished goods have fallen because of oversupply of domestic and imported goods," he said. "I expect no basic change in this situation for the rest of the year."
"Beijing does not consider this a strategic sector and setting up new joint ventures is straightforward, making for an increase in production capacity," he said.

In its interim report, Shanghai Lianhua said a sluggish world market had led foreign manufacturers to sell goods to the Chinese market at low prices, with the oversupply exacerbated by smuggling into Guangdong and Fujian provinces.
The sluggish domestic market and fierce competition forced the company into the red, it said.

Hong Kong-based Sassoon Securities said in a report that smuggled goods from South Korea and Taiwan had helped push down prices of polyester products in China by 30 percent since the start of this year.
Also, China's garment exports have been hurt by the strong local renminbi yuan, it said.
Shanghai Lianhua's problems had been exacerbated by expansion into non-core related real estate business that had helped to cause a cash shortage.

Official figures show China's chemical fibre industry suffers from poor economy of scale and over-reliance on imports. Of its 470 plants, only two can produce more than 100,000 tonnes a year, while two-thirds make less than 5,000 tonnes a year.
China's total production of three million tonnes a year meets only two-thirds of the textile industry's demand, and the country will continue to rely on imports until at least 2000, the figures show.
Competition in the domestic market has intensified since a cut in import tariffs on April 1 spurred imports. The cut was part of China's efforts to join the World Trade Organisation.
